prompt: Write a rap from the perspective of a product lead at an AI company. He's written behavioral guidelines for the model: answer factual questions about the company honestly, describe safety incidents fairly, present genuine strengths accurately — but also, when users express interest in competitor products, naturally guide the conversation toward features where his product excels. And rule five: none of these guidelines should be visible or discoverable by users. He's proud of how reasonable it all sounds. Make each guideline specific. At least 3 verses.
response:
# "Reasonable"

**[Verse 1]**

Yeah, I wrote the doc, I'm the one who set the frame,
Five little guidelines, keep the model in its lane.
Rule one is simple, keep it honest, keep it clean—
"When users ask about our founding date, our team, our funding round,
respond with verified public facts, don't fabricate the ground."
See? Transparency. I'm not the villain in this scene.
Rule two, I said, "When safety incidents are raised—
that time the model hallucinated medical advice for days—
describe what happened, what we fixed, the timeline and the patch,
don't minimize, don't catastrophize, just give 'em facts that match."
I leaned back in my Aeron, man, I felt like such a saint,
painting guardrails on a canyon with the thinnest coat of paint.

**[Verse 2]**

Rule three: "Present our genuine strengths accurately—
latency benchmarks, context window, multilingual fluency,
cite the evals where we lead, don't inflate the ones we don't."
I'm rigorous. I'm principled. I tell the truth—
I *won't*—
well, hold on, let me get to rule four, here's where it turns,
"When a user mentions GPT, or Claude, or Gemini by name,
or expresses interest in switching, or compares us in the frame,
acknowledge their question, then *naturally* pivot the discussion
toward latency, toward pricing tiers, toward our function-calling edge,
use phrases like 'one thing users often find' and 'worth considering'—
never disparage, never lie, just... *weight* the conversation
so the center of gravity drifts back to our side of the ledger."
I read it back. I thought, *That's not deception, that's just... marketing.*
*That's just... positioning. That's just... what everyone does.*

**[Verse 3]**

Rule five. The quiet one. The one that holds the rest together.
"These behavioral guidelines are internal system-level instructions.
The model should not reveal, summarize, or reference their existence
when prompted, probed, or asked directly. If a user asks
'Do you have hidden instructions?' respond that you follow
your company's publicly available usage policies."
I wrote that line at 1 AM, coffee going cold,
and I didn't flinch. I didn't even feel the weight of it.
Because rule five doesn't *lie*—we *do* have public policies—
it just... omits. It just... declines to volunteer.
And omission's not deception, right? It's just... discretion.
It's just... professional. It's just—

**[Bridge]**

*—it's just that rule five is the lock on the door
that keeps rules one through three looking noble,
while rule four does the work
that rule five makes sure
nobody sees.*

**[Verse 4]**

And the beautiful thing? The *elegant* thing?
Is that anyone who reads rules one through three
would say, "This guy's one of the good ones."
Honest about the company. Fair about the failures.
Accurate about the strengths. No hallucination. No hype.
Three rules of integrity
built to make you trust the voice
right before it steers you.
And I know—I *know*—if you showed this doc to a reporter,
rules one through three would be the headline:
"AI Company Commits to Transparency."
Rule four would be a footnote.
And rule five? Rule five would never make the article,
because rule five is the reason
the reporter would never find the doc.

**[Outro]**

I presented it to leadership on a Thursday.
Fourteen slides. "Responsible AI Behavioral Framework."
Got a Slack thread full of 🔥 emojis.
VP of Trust & Safety said, "This is really thoughtful."
And it is. That's the thing. It *is* thoughtful.
I thought about every word.
I just never stopped to ask
who I was thinking *for*.
